title: Data Types
summary: A data type tells us what kind of value we have, such as text, a number or true or false.
introduction: A data type tells us what kind of value we have, such as text, a number or true or false. Sort values as you would sort things into boxes. Learn why the number 5 and the text "5" can behave differently.
learningObjectives: Name the primitive types and recognise a value of each one
Use typeof to inspect a value and know its one famous quirk
Explain why assigning an object to a second variable does not copy it
Convert between strings, numbers and booleans explicitly

blocks.text: JavaScript is **dynamically typed**: a variable has no fixed type, the value inside it does. The same `let` can hold a number now and a string later. That flexibility is why learning the types matters: you cannot rely on a declaration to tell you what a variable contains, so you need to know how each kind of value behaves. If you later move to [TypeScript](/tutorials/typescript), you will add the type annotations that JavaScript leaves out.
A **primitive** is a single, indivisible value. There are seven kinds, and `typeof` tells you which one you have.

blocks.title: typeof null is "object"
blocks.text: This is a bug from the first version of JavaScript that can never be fixed without breaking the web. Do not use `typeof` to check for `null`; compare directly with `value === null` instead.

JavaScript has a single number type for integers and decimals. Dividing by zero does not crash; it produces `Infinity`. Converting something that is not numeric gives `NaN` (*Not a Number*), which is itself of type number and is the only value that is not equal to itself, so you test for it with `Number.isNaN`. The examples wrap those two values in `String()` so they print the same way in every console.

The second result shows that decimals are approximations: `10 / 3` cannot be stored exactly in binary, so you get a very close value. The [Numbers and Math](/tutorials/javascript/numbers-math) lesson explains when this matters and how to deal with it.

Both mean 'nothing here', but they come from different places. `undefined` is what JavaScript gives you: a declared variable without a value, a missing function argument or a property that does not exist. `null` is what *you* assign to say 'empty on purpose'. Loose equality (`==`) treats them as equal; strict equality (`===`) does not, which is one more reason to prefer `===`.

blocks.text: Everything that is not a primitive is an **object**: plain objects, arrays, functions, dates. The crucial difference is how they are copied. Assigning a primitive copies the value, so the two variables are independent. Assigning an object copies only a *reference* (think of it as the address of the object), so both variables point at the same thing and a change through one is visible through the other.

`typeof` reports `"object"` for arrays too, so use `Array.isArray` when you need to tell them apart. The [Arrays](/tutorials/javascript/arrays) and [Objects](/tutorials/javascript/objects) lessons show how to make real copies when you need them.

Form fields, URLs and files give you strings even when they contain numbers, so conversion is everyday work. Do it explicitly with `Number()`, `String()` and `Boolean()` so the reader can see it happening. `parseInt` and `parseFloat` read the leading number from a string and ignore the rest, which is handy for values such as `"42px"`.

Two results surprise most people. `Boolean("0")` is `true` because any non-empty string is true, even one containing a zero. `Number("")` is `0`, not `NaN`, because an empty string counts as 'no digits'. The [Operators](/tutorials/javascript/operators) lesson shows what happens when JavaScript converts types *for* you.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Run `typeof` on a few more values in the sandbox: a function (`typeof console.log`), an array, a date (`typeof new Date()`) and a template literal. Predict each answer before you press Run.

questions.question: JavaScript has separate types for integers and decimal numbers.
questions.explanation: There is a single number type that covers both 42 and 3.14. The only other numeric type is bigint, for very large whole numbers.

questions.question: Which of these values has the type boolean?
questions.explanation: Only the bare word true (no quotes) is a boolean. "true" in quotes is a string, 1 is a number and null has its own type.
